text: This tiny yellow bird saved countless miners... and it worked underground for seventy-five years.
Down in the coal mines, the deadliest killer was invisible. Carbon monoxide. No smell. No color.
By the time a miner felt dizzy... it was usually too late.
After an explosion, this poison spread through the tunnels, and it often killed more miners than the blast itself.
So in the eighteen nineties, a scientist named John Haldane tested those poison gases... on himself.
He tried mice too. But a canary was easier to watch... and it sang all day long.
And he found the perfect alarm. A canary.
Canaries are tiny and breathe really fast, so the gas hits them first.
If the canary stopped singing, or fell off its perch, everyone got out. Fast.
By nineteen eleven, British law made the bigger mines keep birds underground.
But here's the twist. The miners didn't want them to die. They used a special cage with an oxygen tank, to bring them back to life.
When the bird fainted, a miner shut the little door, opened the oxygen valve... and the canary woke right back up.
The canaries kept their jobs until nineteen eighty-six, when electronic detectors finally took over.
Did you learn something new? Like, and subscribe.
